title: Decidability of termination for one left- and right-linear term rule
formal: Is there an algorithm that, given one first-order rewrite rule \(\ell\to r\) over a finite ranked signature, with both \(\ell\) and \(r\) linear, decides whether its unrestricted rewrite relation terminates on every finite term?
why: The problem asks whether simultaneous linearity of the two sides imposes enough structure to make global termination decidable for a single rule. It probes how little rewrite syntax can already encode unbounded computation, beyond the established left-linear and string-only boundaries.
status_note: The original source retains the left-and-right-linear one-rule termination question. The checked 2024 undecidability paper concerns existence of linear interpretation proofs, not the variable-linear termination property itself. No resolution of the exact latter question was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 later-work check.

progress.text: Dauchet establishes the cited undecidability boundary when only left linearity is required.
The RTALooP problem asks for decidability when both sides of the single rule are linear.
Mitterwallner, Middeldorp and Thiemann prove undecidability of certain linear-interpretation termination tests, a different property from termination of a variable-linear rule.

importance.reason: A precise minimal-syntax decidability boundary for rewriting, retaining the existing score while distinguishing variable-linearity from restrictions on termination proof methods.

sentences: The input is one first-order rewrite rule whose left and right sides each use every variable at most once.
The rule may be applied at any position in any finite term, with ordinary syntactic substitutions.
The question asks whether an algorithm can decide absence of every infinite reduction sequence.
Left-linearity alone and the smaller string-rewriting subclass have different known boundaries.
Recent undecidability for linear-interpretation proof methods must not be confused with linearity of the rule itself.

definitions: A ranked signature \(\Sigma\) consists of finitely many function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are finite ordered trees over \(\Sigma\) and a countably infinite set of variables. A term is linear if each variable occurs at most once in that term; occurrences are counted separately on the two sides of a rule. The left side \(\ell\) must not be a variable and every variable of \(r\) must occur in \(\ell\); variables may be erased, but may not be duplicated on either side or newly introduced on the right. A substitution maps variables to finite terms. A one-step rewrite replaces one occurrence of \(\ell\sigma\) by \(r\sigma\) inside an arbitrary term context, for some substitution \(\sigma\). The same single rule may be used at any position and any number of times. Matching is syntactic; no equations, types, binding operations or restrictions such as innermost-only rewriting are present. Termination means there is no infinite chain \(u_0\to u_1\to u_2\to\cdots\) starting from any finite term, including terms with variables. It is not only existence of one terminating reduction, termination from one designated input, or absence of short cycles. If a rewrite returns the same term, it is still a step and can witness nontermination by repetition. The finite signature, symbol arities, variables and both finite term trees are explicitly encoded and form the algorithm’s input. A decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid input rule and answers the global termination question exactly; no complexity bound is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for every valid rule linear on both sides, or prove in Lean that this restricted global termination problem is undecidable. A single nonterminating example does not prove undecidability. A decision procedure for string rules, a bounded search for loops, or a test for whether one specific interpretation proves termination does not settle the full proposition.

context_blocks.text: Linearity controls variable repetition, not the number of function symbols. Both \(f(x)\to x\) and \(f(x)\to f(f(x))\) are linear on each side. The first decreases term size at every step and terminates; the second can grow forever. Thus the input class includes both possible answers even with unary function symbols.

Dauchet’s 1991 question explicitly requires both left and right linearity. The source cites undecidability for one rule with only left linearity, so omitting the right-side restriction would replace the open question by a known harder model.

One-rule string rewriting is a special case, represented by unary function symbols with a shared tail variable. Its unresolved termination question is therefore related but does not cover the branching first-order terms admitted here. The source separately discusses confluence, which is another property and is not part of the present target.

The 2024 paper Linear Termination is Undecidable studies whether termination can be certified by linear polynomial interpretations. Here “linear” describes the proof interpretation, whereas this card uses it for occurrence of variables in a rule. The paper’s undecidability result is not a resolution of the question merely because the titles share the word linear.

Indeed, that paper can make the interpretation-existence question undecidable even within systems already known to terminate by another polynomial interpretation. This emphasizes the difference between deciding actual termination and deciding whether a particular proof method succeeds.

Global termination quantifies over every finite term and every choice of redex. A collection of successful test reductions or the absence of a repeated term in bounded exploration does not establish it. Likewise, a rule may fail to terminate by unbounded growth without ever repeating a term.
